newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French love affair with supertrains runs off rails.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French love affair with supertrains runs off rails.

text.p: France's love affair with the Train a Grande Vitesse (TGV) has finally gone off the financial rails.

Hugely popular with travellers, the supertrains that whizz across the countryside at cruising speeds of 300 km (190 miles) an hour, bringing Brussels and Lyon within two hours of Paris, have crashed through the buffers of public finances.
Since the first TGV line opened in 1981, the sleek orange or blue locomotives with their flattened noses have symbolised the breathtaking modernisation of France's public infrastructure.
But the Transport Ministry has now admitted it can no longer afford to go on building new TGV lines in these times of budget cuts to qualify for a single European currency.

And France's Court of Auditors has reported that the SNCF state railway inflated passenger forecasts to justify the cost of building the northern TGV network in the early 1990s, and that construction firms carved up tenders for building the tracks at an inflated cost to the public purse.
In unusually blunt language, Court of Auditors president Pierre Joxe this month called it a "swindle".

The TGV is also facing local resistance for the first time over the 24 billion French franc ($4.6 billion) extension of the line from Paris to the southern port city of Marseille, slicing through vineyards and scenic riversides in the Provence region.
Defying Paris technocrats, opponents have blocked rail lines and staged demonstrations from Valence to Avignon, where walls are festooned with anti-TGV slogans and threats of sabotage.

Yet corners of France not served by the TGV, such as the eastern city of Strasbourg, are clamouring for the supertrain in the belief -- not entirely borne out by experience -- that it is a springboard to economic development.
The TGV-North line, opened in 1993 in the midst of France's first postwar recession, has yet to turn the northern industrial rust belt into a hive of new enterprise.

The TGV has rearranged French geography. But by halving the travelling time, it has made commuting to Paris a practical option and arguably drained economic activity from towns now within an hour of the already dominant capital.
Britanny, the Loire Valley, the North and the Alps are now a hop-skip-and-jump from the Paris region, where 10 million of France's 58 million citizens live.
But the Pyrenees in the south, Alsace-Lorraine in the east and the central Auvergne region are as distant as ever, and thus further away in relative terms.

Two government-commissioned expert reports released this month concluded that a 1992 masterplan to extend the TGV's tentacles to the east, southwest and around the Mediterranean coast cannot be carried out with current resources and suggested the programme be slowed down and radically modified.

Former SNCF chairman Philippe Rouvillois recommended that France switch from the costly method of building special tracks and adopt the so-called tilting train or Pendolino pioneered by Italy's Fiat Ferroviaria, which runs on normal rail lines.

The tilt train may be slower than the TGV, which is made by the Franco-British company GEC-Alsthom, but it runs on old regional networks as well as on special fast tracks. The snag is it isn't French and the Gaullist government would rather have a French firm manufacture the technology than import it.
Junior transport minister Anne-Marie Idrac insisted this month that the TGV programme, the envy of many European countries, would go ahead, although at a slower pace.
"The TGV programme must continue but progress must be compatible with the financial resources that the nation can afford," she said.

Earlier this year, the government agreed to relieve the SNCF of 125 billion francs ($24.2 billion) in debt as part of a rescue package for the loss-making railway. Most of that debt was incurred in building the TGV network.
"The TGV is a typically French saga of technological success and financial disaster," said RTL radio economic commentator Jean-Yves Hollinger.
Idrac said it would take a generation to complete plans to add 2,300 km (1,430 miles) to the existing 1,300 km (810 miles).

Supporters of the TGV are calling for greater government subsidies to keep the programme going at its planned rate, warning that environment-friendly, fuel-efficient railways will otherwise lose out to motorways and air travel.

The SNCF is already suffering falling passenger numbers. It began with the launch of an over-complex automated reservation system known as Socrates three years ago and was aggravated by a 24-day rail strike last year and economic stagnation.

A price war unleashed by competition on domestic air routes has undercut the railways' attractiveness, leading new SNCF chairman Louis Gallois to announce his intention of cutting prices wherever necessary.
"We have got to stop losing market share to competition from roads and airways and start winning back customers," he said in an interview with the newspaper Le Monde.

Gallois acknowledged that experts had concluded the planned TGV-East line to Strasbourg would be less profitable than previously forecast but said it was up to the government to factor that into a political decision.
Also at stake are high-speed rail links to southern Germany, Austria and eastern Europe which have strong political value. ($1=5.210 French Franc)
